title: Why Is the US Town of Point Roberts Trapped by Canada?

shots.vo: So why is Point Roberts cut off? It began in 1846.
shots.title: Since *1846*

shots.vo: On North America's Pacific coast, Canada and the United States meet at the sea.
For about 2,000 kilometres west of Lake of the Woods, the border follows one line: the 49th parallel.
At its western end, the line crosses a small peninsula that hangs south from Vancouver's suburbs.
The top belongs to Canada. The bottom tip, south of the line, belongs to the United States.
Water surrounds that tip on three sides, with the Strait of Georgia to the west and Boundary Bay to the east.
Its only land border, about five kilometres long, is shared with the Canadian community of Tsawwassen.
On one side are suburban streets; on the other, quiet roads, beaches and holiday cabins among the firs.
shots.prompt: Wide aerial painting of a small peninsula town in the Pacific Northwest: on one side tidy suburban streets with rows of houses, on the other a quiet winding road, a sandy beach and small holiday cabins among tall Douglas firs, soft summer light, no people, no logos, no readable text, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package

shots.vo: To reach the rest of Washington State by car, you first cross into Canada at the Point Roberts gate.
Then you drive north and east through Delta in British Columbia, around Boundary Bay, about 40 kilometres in all.
Then you cross back into the US at Blaine, the first American town on the mainland side.
That means two border checks each way, with passports, for a trip to the dentist or a hardware store.
School makes it a daily trip, because older pupils go to middle and high school in Blaine, on the far side of Boundary Bay.
So a teenager leaves the US, enters Canada, re-enters the US, and does it all again going home.
That is four international border crossings in one school day, on every day of the school year.

So the real question is not how the town gets by. It is why the line falls right here.

shots.vo: In 1791, Spanish sailors charting this coast saw the peninsula from the water and marked it as an island.
A year later, British captain George Vancouver sailed past and named it Point Roberts, after a fellow officer, Henry Roberts.
Later, Britain and the US both claimed Oregon Country, from today's California-Oregon line north to Russian Alaska, at 54°40'.
An 1818 treaty drew the 49th parallel east of the Rocky Mountains and left the west open to both.

document.title: Convention of 1818 between the United States and Great Britain, 20 October 1818, Article III
document.highlight: ...shall... be free and open, for the term of ten years... to the vessels, citizens, and subjects of the two powers

shots.vo: Renewed in 1827, that shared arrangement lasted almost thirty years, while settlers and fur traders from both countries moved in.
In his inaugural address in March 1845, President James Polk called the American claim to Oregon 'clear and unquestionable'.

shots.vo: Britain, whose Hudson's Bay Company ran the fur trade there, wanted the line much further south, along the Columbia River.
Between the two claims lay more than 900 kilometres of coast, from the Columbia River north to latitude 54°40'.
In June 1846, the two governments agreed to a compromise.

shots.vo: The Oregon Treaty ran the line 'along the said forty-ninth parallel' to the channel beside Vancouver Island.

document.title: Oregon Treaty, signed 15 June 1846, Article I
document.highlight: westward along the said forty-ninth parallel of north latitude to the middle of the channel which separates the continent from Vancouver's Island

shots.prompt: Duotone archival plate, dark slate and one muted orange: a handwritten treaty sheet with a ribbon and seal, quill beside it; top third dark and plain

shots.vo: Out at sea, the negotiators bent the line south around Vancouver Island, so Britain kept the whole island.
But on land, nobody made an exception for the small peninsula poking south across the parallel.
Historians generally think the negotiators, working far away in London and Washington, simply overlooked it.

shots.vo: With that, a straight line on paper cut off the tip, and Point Roberts became part of the United States.

map.label: 1846: the tip goes to the USA

shots.vo: According to local histories, British officials suggested the US give the tip up, but Washington did not agree.
shots.prompt: Duotone archival plate, dark slate and one muted orange: a sealed letter being handed across a desk between two gloved hands, 1850s office, no faces, no readable text, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package

shots.vo: Instead, in 1859 the US set the whole tip aside as a military reserve, though no fort was ever built.
Meanwhile, joint British and American survey teams had been marking the line on the ground since 1857.
shots.prompt: Duotone archival plate, dark slate and one muted orange: survey tents and a theodolite on a forested bluff above the sea, 1850s; top third dark and plain

shots.vo: In 1861, they set a granite marker at Point Roberts.
The line was now marked on the ground itself, and its course past Point Roberts has not moved since.
Settlers came anyway, and in the 1890s Icelandic families arrived, fishing and farming on the reserved land.
Salmon canneries and fish traps made this shore one of the busiest fishing spots on the coast in the early 1900s.
shots.prompt: Early 1900s Pacific Northwest shore with a wooden salmon cannery on pilings, fish traps in the water and fishing boats at the dock, workers seen only from behind or in silhouette, overcast light, period-accurate, no logos, no readable text, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package

shots.vo: In 1908, the reserve was finally opened, and families could claim the land they had worked for years.
After 1960, a new ferry terminal and growing suburbs at Tsawwassen brought Vancouver's crowds right up to the fence.
Canadians bought summer cabins on the American side, and the town grew around them.

shots.vo: In 1971, both governments asked their joint commission, the International Joint Commission, to study the town's future.

document.title: International Joint Commission, Point Roberts Reference, 1971
document.highlight: The governments of Canada and the United States ask the Commission to examine the problems of Point Roberts.

shots.prompt: Duotone archival plate, dark slate and one muted orange: a bound government report on a 1970s office desk, a coastline map pinned to the wall behind; top third dark and plain

shots.vo: The map showed the proposed park zone around the tip, but it was never drawn into law, and the border stayed on the 49th parallel.
Today, the town lives mostly on traffic from the north, not from the rest of America to the south.
Local officials say most property owners in Point Roberts are Canadian, many of them with holiday homes.
shots.prompt: Duotone archival plate, dark slate and one muted orange: a row of shuttered holiday homes on a bluff above the sea in winter light, no faces, no readable text, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package

shots.vo: Many Canadians rent American mailboxes here, so online orders from US shops arrive without cross-border shipping.
Others cross for fuel and groceries, and the town's few shops depend on those Canadian customers.

shots.vo: Downtown Vancouver lies about 30 kilometres north of the border gate in a straight line, so Point Roberts sits beside a big city.
Statistics Canada counted about 2.6 million people in that metro area in 2021, against about 1,200 in Point Roberts.

shots.vo: The Point Roberts crossing is staffed by both countries, every hour of every day of the year.
For residents, that one gate is the front door to doctors, jobs, the airports and the rest of America.
Then, on 21 March 2020, the US and Canada closed their land border to non-essential travel.
Residents could still pass through Canada to reach the US mainland, but Canadian visitors stopped coming.

headline.text: US–Canada land border shut to non-essential trips

shots.vo: Whatcom County ran a small passenger boat to Bellingham, so residents could reach the US without crossing Canada.
Point Roberts was cut off from most of its Canadian visitors for almost twenty months.
Canada reopened to vaccinated Americans on 9 August 2021, and the US land border reopened on 8 November.

shots.vo: Then, in 2025, a trade dispute between the two countries reached the town's single gate once again.
Statistics Canada reported that Canadians' return car trips from the US fell about 35% in April 2025.

shots.vo: Many Canadians said they were staying home in response to US tariffs and talk of annexing Canada.

shots.vo: The US government said its tariffs were about border security, drug trafficking and protecting American jobs.
Caught in between, Point Roberts has no say in either capital's choices, yet it feels them first.
Border agencies have their own case: every crossing must be checked, whether the traveller lives one kilometre away or a thousand.
Residents can apply for trusted-traveller cards like NEXUS, which speed things up, but they must still stop.
shots.prompt: Duotone archival plate, dark slate and one muted orange: a hand holding a plain card out of a car window toward a booth, close on the hand only, no readable text, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package

shots.vo: So what could actually change the map for Point Roberts? There are three possible paths.
The first path is a sea link: a regular boat across Boundary Bay to Blaine or Bellingham.
That would give residents a route to the US mainland with no border stop, but someone must pay to run it.

map.label: No border stop, but who pays?

shots.vo: On the map, the town would gain an American lifeline, yet it would still sit on Canada's doorstep.
The second path is a transfer to Canada, which would erase the anomaly with one new line.
Neither government has proposed it, as far as is publicly known, and any such change would need a new treaty between the two countries.
shots.prompt: Duotone archival plate, dark slate and one muted orange: an empty negotiating table with two blank folders and two chairs facing each other, tall windows, no readable text, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package

shots.vo: Residents vote in US elections and send their children to US schools; a transfer would change all of that.
The third path is a special status, such as the shared international park studied in the 1970s.
A shared zone could make life easier for locals, but both countries would have to give up some control.
Or nothing changes at all, which is exactly what has happened for 180 years.
In that time, the town has lived through two world wars, a long border closure and a trade dispute.
shots.prompt: Duotone archival plate, dark slate and one muted orange: the granite boundary obelisk at dusk with a modern fence behind it, sea beyond; top third dark and plain

shots.vo: Which path would you choose if you lived here: a boat, a new flag, or a shared park?
Point Roberts is not really trapped by Canada; it is held by a ruler line that ignored the land beneath it.
And it is not the only one: about 2,000 kilometres east, where the 49th parallel begins at Lake of the Woods, sits another.
Minnesota's Northwest Angle lies just north of that line, a slice of America you can reach by road only through Canada.
